requirement: The harness generates the inputs that existing tools take and drives those tools. It contains no instruction-set simulator, assembler, linker, compiler, firmware or operating system of its own.
verified_by: Wheel census (PRV-04); review of each iteration

requirement: Every generated or extended instruction set runs in QEMU.

The toolchain for every generated instruction set is GNU binutils and GCC as cross tools; the harness generates only their inputs: assembler macros, opcode entries, intrinsics and machine-description patterns.
Firmware and operating systems come from paras and the Parashakti stack. The harness builds and boots them unchanged in derived builds and writes neither.
The build starts from the author's existing work, retrieved from the forge and pinned by commit, before anything is designed.
The build is carried out by an external implementer in numbered iterations against this document, with acceptance decided by commands and their records.
The programme extends to mechanical, analogue electronic, quantum and optical substrates beside digital electronic ones. Molecular and biochemical substrates are outside it.
Mechanical and analogue computers are realised at least in simulation, by simulators that an external implementer builds with free and open-source tools.
Builds are web first: plain JavaScript that runs in a browser with no build step. JavaScript libraries are used only when paras and BURP can ingest their sources.

The programme is delivered as one package: the Sovereignty Architecture, this MRD, the Implementation Guidelines, the Repository Map, the Build Plan and the Test Plan, with briefs for the implementers.

Binary and balanced ternary both run, through every lane where the lane applies. Binary is the performance baseline: every performance figure is reported beside the binary implementation of the same computation on the same target (RD5).

Every combination of representation, substrate, target and language is a separately buildable cell; a cell depends on another only through a stated prerequisite, so the work divides among implementers without waiting on the whole (the build matrix of document 00).
Nothing is installed on the host. Every tool runs inside Docker containers that are created once and kept.
Every script works inside the folder it is run from and writes nothing outside it; temporary files stay inside that folder and never go to /tmp.

Legacy implementations are read-only oracles. The harness never edits, regenerates or replaces Hindawi's transducers, Romenagri, APCISR, AyeHandSum or any other legacy source; derived builds live in the harness's work tree.
verified_by: Oracle tree hashes before and after every run

requirement: Upstream projects stay unbroken: patches apply to pinned trees in derived builds, and the harness never modifies the paras forks in hmnsq.
No report says that something does not work unless a recorded execution shows it; every failure is reported as the command, its exit code and its output.
Legacy pipelines run through their own drivers. Hindawi's composing pipeline runs through its shaili drivers, never as one transducer read on its own.

Gates refuse only on what a release needs: the expected base, the built payload, the repository's own tests and contract checks, secrets, oversized files and version agreement. Every other check reports and never refuses.
Claims about the harness's own work use AyeKnow states. A value that is not known is recorded as not established, with its reason, and is never filled with a guess.
Every tool's --version and --help output, the README and the pages carry the copyright line, the licence and the trademark notices.
Every artefact carries the author's copyright line (‘© 1993–2026 Abhishek Choudhary. All rights reserved.’) and the affiliation AyeAI. No published material names an AI as author or contributor.
Every received document is cleaned of invisible characters before it is read; the original is kept byte-identical.
The implementer never pushes, publishes, mints or creates repositories. Seeding and minting are the author's acts, through his estate procedure on his machine.
Tools and releases are held to the rigour of a critical system: every requirement traces to a test, every test is shown to fail before it passes, and builds are reproducible.
Every decision considers major and low-resource economies alike; no country, language, script, numeral system or locale is the default.
A tool's interface is read (its --help, its source or a recorded run) before the harness drives it; no flag, function or patch anchor is recalled from memory.
Output is verbose and plainly presented; no step's output is discarded.
Hindawi's construct tables belong to Hindawi. The harness emits new mnemonics and constructs as a list for Hindawi's own process and never edits the tables.

One meta-model describes every representation in sixteen sections: identity, domain, structure, encoding, decoding, semantics, operations, composition, transformations, constraints, substrate, interfaces, verification, generation, evolution and provenance (section 9.3).
Specifications are human-readable YAML validated against a JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) meta-model. A JSON view, where one is produced, is labelled as an alternative.

Each operation's meaning is given by exactly one reference function in a restricted subset of C11: pure, fixed-width integer types, no allocation, no input or output, no undefined behaviour. That function is the single semantic source for software targets, QEMU helpers and the HLS route.
Every field has a stable path (specification identifier plus JSON Pointer) and a hash of its canonical form.
A value not yet established is written as not_established with its reason; the validator and every generator refuse to consume it and name it.
The provenance section names the oracle (repository, commit, path), the extraction method and the evidence state.
The first build covers five families: numeric, script structure, transliteration, symbolic pipeline and machine (instruction extensions and standalone machines).
The specification vocabulary is ingestible by paras, so specifications can be read and written in any Hindawi language with an exact round trip.
Specifications carry semantic versions; the evolution section classes each change as compatible or breaking; instruction encodings follow the allocation ledger (ISA-04).
Each legacy asset has an oracle runner that builds and runs it from its pinned commit inside a container, through its own build system and drivers.
Oracle corpora come first from the asset's own samples, then from generated inputs, then from multilingual corpora in the estate (ILM and tajziya packages); each corpus is hashed.

Extracting a specification from an oracle is descriptive: every extracted rule is confirmed by executing the oracle on the corpus, and where extraction and oracle disagree, the oracle wins and the disagreement is recorded.

Assets that the received documents describe and the author's record does not show (the machine-stack explainer, the APCISR WebAssembly trace, AyeHandSum's mechanisms) are located at intake. An asset not found is recorded with every place searched, and no stand-in is built for it.

For a representation with a legacy implementation, the legacy source is the implementation. The harness builds it unmodified for native, WebAssembly and Python targets and generates only glue: bindings, build files and vectors.

For a representation without a legacy implementation, the harness generates C11 sources from the specification and its reference functions, with WebAssembly builds, a JavaScript loader and Python bindings, using existing toolchains.
Generation is deterministic: the same inputs give byte-identical outputs. Generated files carry the specification hash and generator version, and no timestamps.

Every generated file carries the licence of its destination: the harness's licence in its own tree, and the licence the upstream accepts for files compiled into it (GPL-2.0-or-later for QEMU and Linux, GPL-3.0-or-later for binutils and GCC).

Candidate tables for scripts or transliterations outside the author's canon are harness outputs, kept in its tree and marked candidate. Adopting them into APCISR, Romenagri or Hindawi is the author's act.
Every generator declares the specification paths it reads, and the harness records the paths it actually reads. A read outside the declaration fails the generator's own test.

The dependency graph is a plain-text edge list under version control, with seven edge types: depends_on, implements, transforms, preserves, accelerates, requires and validates. A rendering is generated from it.

Ninja executes the graph. Each declared read is materialised as a slice file rewritten only when its canonical content changes, and generator steps restat their outputs, so a change rebuilds exactly its dependants.
The impact command reports, before any build, which artefacts a proposed change will regenerate and which conformance cells will rerun; the following build confirms that exactly that set changed.

Demonstrator D2 holds for four changes: (a) one AyeHandSum encoding rule, regenerating its encoder, decoder, vectors and dependent instruction and hardware artefacts only; (b) one APCISR grid rule in a derived build, regenerating that script's tables, builds and conformance only; (c) one new operation in a specification, generating its glue, instruction candidate and tests only; (d) the trit encoding of the balanced ternary specification, regenerating its software, QEMU helpers, intrinsics and hardware units and nothing in the script lane.
A deliberate change against a legacy oracle carries an expected-divergence set. Conformance passes when the observed differences equal that set and fails on any other difference.

Tier A extends a RISC-V base profile with custom extensions in the custom opcode space. Base profiles mirror the SHAKTI core classes that Parashakti targets, with parameters read from the ingested SHAKTI sources at intake; the working profiles are RV64GC and RV32IMAC.

First-build Tier A instructions are register-to-register operations with no new architectural state and no memory access. An instruction with state or memory access needs an architecture decision record first.

Candidate instructions come from specification operations marked as candidates. A candidate is promoted only when its measured benefit is recorded against the base instruction set running the same reference function: dynamic instruction count from QEMU's counting plugin and, from M5, hardware resources. Candidates without recorded benefit are kept and not promoted.

Encodings are allocated once, in an allocation ledger kept in the tree. Allocations are checked against the RISC-V opcode database (a collision with a standard extension is refused) and against the vendor extensions the pinned binutils knows (a collision is reported). Regeneration never moves an allocated encoding.

The QEMU generator emits decodetree files, translation functions, helper declarations and helper bodies that call the reference functions, a CPU property that guards the extension, and build entries. It applies them to a pinned QEMU tree through exact-anchor patches that stop and name the anchor when it has moved.
With the CPU property off, every new instruction raises an illegal-instruction exception: SIGILL in user mode, a trap in system mode.
The zero-patch path works with stock GNU tools: generated assembler macros use the .insn directive, and generated C intrinsics are inline assembly built on it.
The patch path generates binutils opcode entries, extension registration and gas tests, so the assembler and disassembler know every mnemonic. It builds from pinned sources in its own container.
The patch path generates GCC builtins, machine-description patterns and the -march extension name for promoted instructions.
Sail definitions of the new instructions for the RISC-V Sail model, as a second reference; LLVM TableGen definitions for the LLVM carried by Parashakti.
The generator emits the new mnemonics as a construct list in the form Hindawi's construct tables take, for Hindawi's own localisation process (GOV-17).
The zero-patch lane uses distribution packages of the RISC-V GNU cross toolchain and QEMU inside a container. The patch lane builds binutils, GCC and QEMU from pinned sources.

Every upstream source resolves first to its paras fork in hmnsq (the English baseline branch), then to the pinned upstream release, and the run records which was used. The author's paras run of 22 October 2026 recorded binutils-gdb, musl, newlib and bash as stopping at the fork stage; the fallback for these is recorded per run and reported to paras's next round.
Build parallelism is set from measured free memory and processors. Peak memory, disk and time are recorded for every build.

Test programs written in Hindawi languages are compiled through Hindawi's drop-in front end to the cross compiler. Where the front end cannot drive a cross compiler, an issue text for the Hindawi repository records the command, its exit code and its output.
xv6-riscv, from its paras fork or the pinned upstream, boots in qemu-system-riscv64 with the extension enabled, and a user program runs the new instructions with results equal to the vectors.

A minimal Linux kernel with a static initramfs boots on the QEMU virt machine with the extension enabled and runs the same test binary. Firmware resolves to Parashakti's first and to the firmware bundled with the pinned QEMU otherwise; the source used is recorded.
A compatibility matrix records, from executions, which Parashakti operating systems boot on which harness targets. A cell that has not been run reads not established.
Operating-system builds are derived builds in the harness's work tree; the paras forks stay untouched.

For each promoted operation the harness produces synthesisable SystemVerilog and VHDL-2008 units, either generated directly from the specification's tables and bit definitions or produced by an open high-level synthesis tool from the reference function. The route is recorded per unit.
Units are simulated with Verilator and GHDL through one cocotb test per unit that reads the shared vectors.
Units with small input domains are checked exhaustively in simulation or by bounded proof with SymbiYosys.
Yosys reports resources and nextpnr reports timing for at least one low-cost FPGA family with an open flow. These are recorded as measurements, never as claims about silicon.

A coprocessor wrapper conforming to the OpenHW CV-X-IF interface attaches the units to an open core that implements it, and the same compiled test program runs on the Verilated core and in QEMU with equal results (D4).
Integration with a SHAKTI core starts from a study that reads the SHAKTI core sources ingested by Parashakti and records their extension mechanism. No mechanism is assumed.

ASIC hand-off uses jugaad28's descriptors, evidence rungs and open-PDK containers. Units that emulate ternary on binary logic follow the binary flow; native ternary circuits go to zamin, keeping jugaad28's substrate boundary (its invariant J4).
On-board FPGA runs are needs:human packets carried out when a board is at hand, with the board and toolchain versions recorded beside the result.

The script lane instantiates the author's 9-grid model as APCISR defines it, read from APCISR's source and the author's paper at intake and confirmed by him (P6.1). No grid semantics are assumed beyond what is read.

For each script, the generator derives candidate grid tables in APCISR's own table format from the Unicode Character Database, CLDR exemplar sets and, where they exist, the script's Romenagri tables, and builds APCISR itself with them for native and WebAssembly targets.

Per-script conformance compares cluster boundaries and positional classes with HarfBuzz shaping of the same text in a reference font of the Noto family, and with Unicode grapheme cluster rules. Results are published as status per script.
Gaps between a script and the grid model are recorded as findings for the author's ruling. The harness never alters or replaces the model to close a gap.

The lane covers every script in the ILM registry pinned in tajziya. Its first working set spans regions: Devanagari, Tamil, Arabic in Urdu orthography, Khmer, Ethiopic, Tifinagh, Hebrew, Cyrillic and Han.
Native-reader review of rendered samples is a needs:human packet per script. Coverage is published as status and never used as a gate.

The first-build numeric specifications are two's-complement binary integer (the performance baseline), balanced ternary, the dynamic-base encoding of AyeHandSum as extracted at intake, and packed decimal.

Definition of balanced ternary (RD5, decided): two bits per trit (00 is 0, 01 is +1, 10 is -1, 11 is invalid); 32 trits in a 64-bit register and 16 in a 32-bit register; operations negate, add, subtract, multiply (low half), compare, shift by trits, and conversion to and from two's complement. The specification defines the result of overflow, of invalid codes and of out-of-range conversion.
A second trit encoding, as two bit-planes, is specified beside the first and is the change used in D2(d).

Numeric oracles are independent of the reference functions: arbitrary-precision integers (Python or GMP) for ternary and decimal homomorphism checks, Python's decimal module or libdecnumber for decimal, and SoftFloat with TestFloat for any IEEE binary format added later.
Further numeric families follow through the same lanes as later milestones: fixed point, posits, low-precision formats for machine learning and arbitrary precision.

Binary is the performance baseline. A fixed workload set (Embench-IoT kernels and the CMS-03 continuous models as fixed-point programs) runs on RV32 and RV64 in QEMU, on the binary Tier B machine and on a Verilated open core, with dynamic instruction counts, cycles and synthesis figures recorded; emulator counts are never stated as hardware speed.
Binary and balanced ternary run through the software, Tier A, Tier B, hardware and mechanical lanes; packed decimal and the AyeHandSum dynamic base follow wherever measurement promotes them.
Vectors are plain text, one case per line, in hexadecimal fields, with a header naming the specification identifier, version and hash. Every runner reads the same files.

The runners are native C, WebAssembly, Python, QEMU user mode, QEMU system mode under each booted operating system, Verilator, GHDL and core co-simulation. A promoted operation passes only when every applicable runner agrees with the reference on every vector.

Each runner enumerates finite domains exhaustively from the domain description, without storing them, up to a configured bound (working value 1,048,576 cases per operation), restricting operands to their low digits where the full width is larger. Beyond the bound, stored boundary cases from the specification and seeded random cases are used (working value 100,000 per operation), with property-based tests (Hypothesis) on software targets.

Every lane has a mutation self-test that plants specified defects (a table entry, an off-by-one, a wrong funct3, swapped operands, a flipped hardware bit) and shows the conformance suite catching each one. The report gives planted and caught counts.
Round-trip and homomorphism properties of reference functions with small widths are proved by bounded methods (Z3 or a C bounded model checker).
Every run writes a run record: input specification hashes, oracle commits, tool versions, container image digests, output artefact hashes, conformance results and AyeKnow states.
Each run record is also written as an in-toto Statement v1 in Candor's form. Timestamping with OpenTimestamps happens on the author's machine.
Reports are actionable: each finding states what it means, what to do and where.
A generated status page shows the compatibility matrix, script coverage, the wheel census (which external tool did the work at each layer) and AyeKnow states, and reads well on a phone.
satsneha consumes run records in reporting mode only.
RESUME.md is generated from the run records at the end of every run and gives each packet's state with its evidence. It is never edited by hand.

One command-line tool, repsynth, with subcommands doctor, intake, spec check, gen, impact, run, conform, report and selftest. One command runs a whole milestone or iteration end to end (repsynth run --milestone M, repsynth run --iteration N).
The operator's intent is taken once per run. The tool has no irreversible action of its own, so it carries no typed gates beyond confirming the deletion of its own caches.
A run shows live progress (what is running and what remains) and stops and resumes from any stage without repeating completed stages.
doctor is timed, never installs anything on the host and reports what is missing; doctor --build builds the containers once.
A colour terminal status display in the manner of paras, and placement of heavy jobs on chosen processors.
The tool is a Python package installable with pipx; its containers build from Dockerfiles in its tree.
repsynth compile and repsynth capability produce substrate programs and the capability matrix.
After the first fetch, every lane runs offline from caches inside the run folder.
The whole first build fits the reference unit: 16 GB of memory, the disk budget of PRF-02, one heavy build at a time.
Outputs meant for people (WebAssembly builds of representations, the status page, script samples) run in a phone browser without a server.
Hardware routes favour open flows and low-cost boards available worldwide; ASIC routes include open process design kits from more than one country through jugaad28.
The harness's own repository passes paras ingestion with an exact round trip in every Hindawi language, as the stack packages do.
Peak memory, disk and wall time are measured for every build and recorded in the run record.

The disk budget for the working set is a configuration value (working value 8 GB). Before a run, the harness computes each lane's need from recorded peaks (estimates, labelled as such, on a first run), reports any shortfall up front, runs the lanes that fit and says why the others did not run.
Build directories are removed once their artefacts are captured and hashed; clones are shallow where history is not needed; caches are bounded.
Regeneration after a one-field change leaves unaffected lanes unbuilt, and its time is recorded.
Reference containers are built when their lane first needs them and are kept; before a new image is built, the run reports each image's size and the total against free disk.

One parametric machine generator produces two standalone machines from their specifications, a binary word machine and a balanced ternary word machine encoded on a binary host (RD5); each is a new QEMU target with a CPU, decodetree translation, helpers and a minimal board with memory, a UART and an exit device, and both boot bare-metal test images.
Tier B test images are assembled by an existing retargetable assembler (customasm) from a generated instruction definition.

A binutils port for the Tier B machine (assembler, disassembler, and a linker with a minimal ELF backend) is generated from the machine specification and assembles the same sources to identical images.
A GCC port for a Tier B machine lies outside the first build and needs its own amendment to this document.

An application specification declares the representations, precisions and latency an application needs; the harness proposes representation choices and instruction candidates for it and measures them through the same lanes.
Teaching labs package exercises (add an instruction, change an encoding, watch the stack regenerate) for computer architecture and compiler courses, each runnable on one laptop from one command.

One substrate meta-model describes every substrate in fifteen sections: medium, state space, state transitions, operations, observability, controllability, temporal behaviour, noise and uncertainty, resource constraints, interface, units, parameters, capabilities, realisation models and provenance (section 9.9).
A substrate specification is distinct from a representation specification. A realisation record links them: the representation, the substrate, the mechanism and the capability class.

Every physical parameter carries an evidence state: measured (with its record), sourced (with its citation), assumed (stated as an assumption) or not established. Results show the assumed and not-established parameters they depend on.
The first build specifies five substrates: mechanical, analogue electronic, digital electronic, quantum and optical.
Every quantity carries a UCUM unit or is declared dimensionless.

A computational model specification describes a computation without reference to any substrate: state variables, inputs, outputs, transitions and semantics, given as equations for continuous models, as reference functions for discrete models (SPC-03) and as OpenQASM 3 circuits for quantum models.

The restricted expression grammar for equations is defined once, in EBNF, with one parser in the shared web core and generators to Modelica equations and SPICE behavioural expressions; every model's generated forms re-parse to the same syntax tree.

The first computational models are exponential decay, the harmonic oscillator, a damped driven oscillator, the Lorenz system, function generation y = f(x) for a stated set of functions, and balanced ternary addition (NUM-02).

The cross-substrate compiler maps a computational model to a program for each substrate (a mechanism configuration, an analogue patch, an instruction sequence, a quantum circuit, an interferometer mesh), performs the magnitude and time scaling the substrate needs, and records every scale factor.

For every model and substrate the compiler reports exactly one capability class (supported; supported with restrictions; approximate, with its bound; simulation only; not realisable under stated constraints, naming the constraint) and attaches the record that justifies it.
The capability matrix of models by substrates is published on the status page, each cell with its class and record.

A simulated result is recorded as simulated and never as physically realised. A physical claim needs measurements entered with their evidence, on dhancha's rungs (SPEC, MODEL, SIMULATED, BENCH, FLIGHT) or jugaad28's rungs for integrated circuits.

Every simulator and every browser face of the harness is plain JavaScript in ES modules that runs in a current browser with no build step, bundler or transpiler, served from GitHub Pages or any static server.

Third-party JavaScript is vendored as readable, unminified source under vendor/<name>/<version>/ with its licence file, upstream source, version and a sha256 for every file; nothing is fetched from a CDN at run time.

A library or source file is admitted only after BURP returns its sources byte for byte. The admission state of each library (admitted, pending BURP, rejected) is recorded, and every BURP gap is reported with its command, exit code and output for BURP's next round.

Sources use no eval, no new Function and no generated code. WebAssembly appears only when built from sources that are themselves ingested (the C reference functions), never as the only form of a library.
Simulators work offline after first load and on a phone browser. Long runs execute in Web Workers, and a heavy run lowers its resolution rather than freezing the page.

Every simulator exposes one command surface in the browser and in Node.js. Fixed-step results are byte-identical between Node.js and Chromium-based browsers, and within the Test Plan's cross-engine bound on other engines, because ECMAScript does not require correctly rounded transcendental functions.
Every simulator page shows the author's notices, links to its run records and the capability matrix, and exports and imports programs and traces as plain text.

The mechanical simulator (hmnsq/mechsim) simulates computing mechanisms from a mechanism configuration: shafts, gear pairs and trains, differentials, wheel-and-disc integrators, cams and followers, lead screws, ratchets, counter wheels with carry, crank inputs, dials and plotters.

Two levels of model run from one configuration: an ideal kinematic model (constraints and integrator equations) and a lumped dynamic model (inertia, compliance, backlash, friction and integrator slip), every parameter with its evidence state.

Discrete mechanisms (detents, carries, ratchets) simulate exactly. Mechanical binary and balanced ternary adders, with two and three detent positions per wheel, run from their specifications and equal their reference functions on every vector.
Configurations export geometry (involute gears, cams, frames) through JSCAD as STL or 3MF with tolerances recorded. Geometry is a realisation model, not a claim of a working build.

Ideal and lumped results are cross-checked against Modelica models generated from the same configuration and run in OpenModelica in a container; a three-dimensional multibody check with Project Chrono covers at least one gear train and one differential.
The page shows mechanisms moving (2D in SVG or canvas; 3D with three.js), plots outputs against time or input, and the same modules run headless in Node.js.
Differential analyser configurations solve the continuous models of CMS-03 mechanically (D8).

The analogue simulator (hmnsq/anasim) simulates analogue computer programs given as patches: integrators with initial conditions, summers, coefficient potentiometers, inverters, multipliers, comparators, limiters, function generators and sample-and-hold elements, under mode control (initial condition, operate, hold).

Two levels of model run from one patch: ideal computing elements assembled into an ODE system, and non-ideal elements with finite gain and bandwidth, offset, drift, saturation at the machine unit, component tolerances and seeded noise, every parameter with its evidence state.
The patch compiler scales magnitudes to the machine unit and time to the elements' bandwidth, records the factors, and reports any overload with the element and the time at which it occurs.

Patches export SPICE netlists of op-amp realisations, using a generic macro-model rather than any vendor's model, and Modelica models; both run in containers and are compared with the browser results within the Test Plan bounds.
The page shows the patch as a diagram and its traces on a scope view, and the same modules run headless in Node.js.
A bill of materials by generic part class and a breadboard-level netlist form the physical realisation model of a patch.

No new quantum simulator is written. The quantum lane uses Panini Q where its interface covers an operation, an existing browser circuit library for the web face, and Qiskit Aer and QuTiP in a container as references; OpenQASM 3 is the interchange.

Quantum results are compared as state vectors where every simulator exposes them and as measurement distributions otherwise, under the Test Plan's statistical bounds; qubit ordering and phase conventions are recorded and tested.
Panini Q is read at intake and its interface recorded, citing files and lines, before any adapter is designed; Panini Q itself changes only by the author's ruling.

Optical models are linear transfer matrices realised as interferometer meshes by a published decomposition; a later milestone (M13) builds the browser face in hmnsq/optisim and compares it with a photonic reference.
